The port responds.
Is the service healthy?

A controlled investigation from a working baseline through HTTP 503 to verified recovery. Connection checks, application evidence and a clear technical handover.

Same endpoint. Three observed states.

127.0.0.1:56119 /health

  1. 01 / Baseline

    HTTP 200

    Name resolvedTCP connected

    Expected health response

    10:03:27 UTC

  2. 02 / Application fault

    HTTP 503

    Name resolvedTCP connected

    Application unavailable

    10:03:30 UTC

  3. 03 / Recovery verified

    HTTP 200

    Name resolvedTCP connected

    Expected health response

The TCP check passed in all three states. Recovery was confirmed by HTTP 200 and the expected service identity and healthy payload.

Investigation and decisions

  1. Establish the baseline

    Resolve localhost, test the selected TCP port, then inspect the HTTP status and response body. Preserve the result before injecting a fault.

  2. Separate connectivity from application health

    TCP still succeeds while the fixture returns 503. This identifies an application-level failure in this experiment; it does not establish a physical device or external network fault.

  3. Remove the controlled fault and retest

    Change the fixture from unavailable to healthy on the same port. Repeat the manual probes and the bounded checker; retain the recovery record.

  4. Check alternative failure paths

    Stop the owned service and test a reserved nonexistent name separately. Confirm failed prerequisites produce clear findings and skipped downstream checks.

OBSERVED OUTCOME

HTTP 503 → HTTP 200

The recovered run passed local name resolution, TCP connectivity and the expected application health response.

The injected cause is known: a fixture-mode change. These controlled observations are not production uptime or resolution-time statistics.

Communication and technical handover

Example wording based on this lab evidence. These messages were not sent to customers or colleagues.

DURING THE INVESTIGATION

Customer update

“The test service is reachable, but its health endpoint is returning an unavailable response. We have isolated the difference between connectivity and application health. Next, we will restore the test service’s healthy mode and repeat the same checks before confirming recovery.”

FOR THE NEXT ENGINEER

Technical handover

Scope: the local fixture at 127.0.0.1:56119. Localhost resolution and TCP connectivity succeeded during HTTP 503. The controlled trigger was the unavailable fixture mode. Restoring healthy mode produced HTTP 200 with the expected service identity and status. Baseline, fault and recovery records are linked above.

Limits and next checks

  • Localhost resolution does not test an external DNS server. Loopback traffic does not validate a router, WAN, firewall path or physical device.
  • HTTP 503 alone does not explain the cause of a real incident. Outside this controlled fixture, review service logs, dependencies, configuration and the incident time window.
  • A failed TCP check narrows the investigation but does not by itself prove hardware failure. A listening port does not prove the correct application is healthy.
  • Recovery is scoped to the tested endpoint and time. A real service also needs its relevant user journey or transaction checked before closure.
  • Independent practice, Linux log investigation and applying this method to a real support case remain separate learning steps.
